questions.q: As the forecast horizon in a GARCH(1,1) model grows (e.g., 20 days ahead vs. 1 day ahead), what typically happens to the variance forecast, assuming alpha + beta < 1?
options: It grows without bound indefinitely
It flattens out and converges toward the long-run unconditional variance
It immediately drops to zero
It stays frozen at today's exact conditional variance forever
questions.explain: Whenever alpha + beta < 1 (the stationarity condition), the GARCH recursion mean-reverts: forecasts further into the future flatten toward the model's long-run average variance rather than continuing to react to the most recent shock.

questions.q: How should a GARCH-based volatility forecast be evaluated for quality?
options: By checking only its in-sample AIC
By comparing it against realized volatility over the forecasted period, using RMSE/MAE-style metrics, and against a naive benchmark
By checking that alpha + beta equals exactly 1
Forecast quality for volatility models cannot be evaluated
questions.explain: As with price forecasts, volatility forecasts should be scored out-of-sample against what volatility actually turned out to be (realized volatility), using standard error metrics, and compared against a naive benchmark like using today's rolling volatility unchanged.

questions.q: What does a volatility-targeting strategy do when a GARCH forecast indicates volatility has doubled?
options: It doubles the position size to capture more potential return
It roughly halves the position size to keep risk contribution steady
It ignores the forecast and holds the position unchanged
It converts the entire position to cash permanently
questions.explain: Volatility targeting sizes positions inversely to forecast volatility, so when volatility doubles, position size is cut roughly in half, keeping the position's risk contribution approximately constant over time.

questions.q: In the formula VaR_alpha = -(mu + z_alpha * sigma_(t+1)), what role does sigma_(t+1) play when it comes from a GARCH forecast rather than a flat historical standard deviation?
options: It has no effect on the VaR estimate
It lets the VaR estimate adapt to current market conditions, rising ahead of turbulent periods rather than only reacting afterward
It forces VaR to always equal zero
It replaces the need for a confidence level alpha entirely
questions.explain: Using a GARCH-forecast sigma_(t+1), which reacts to recent volatility clustering, lets the VaR estimate rise in anticipation of turbulent periods instead of only increasing after losses have already occurred — unlike a flat, unconditional standard deviation.

questions.q: Why is it important to compare a GARCH volatility forecast against a naive benchmark, such as using today's rolling volatility unchanged as tomorrow's forecast?
options: Because GARCH models are never useful and always underperform the naive benchmark
Because a forecast that cannot beat a simple naive approach out-of-sample is not adding real forecasting value, regardless of how sophisticated it looks in-sample
Because naive benchmarks are required by statsmodels to run GARCH models
Because the naive benchmark is always more accurate for options pricing
questions.explain: This mirrors the price-forecasting principle from earlier in the course: a model's real worth is demonstrated by beating a simple, honest benchmark out-of-sample, not by how good its in-sample fit statistics look.
